paras: The lynching of Pantaleon Miera and Santos Benavides was the hanging of two men at Bernalillo, New Mexico Territory, on the night of Tuesday, December 28, 1880. Later reports attributed Miera's death to vigilantes acting on an accusation of horse stealing. The case drew notice beyond the territory a month later, when Miera was named as one of the men who had killed Colonel Charles Potter of the U.S. Geological Survey.

On December 31, 1880, the Las Vegas Morning Gazette printed a one-line item among its local gleanings giving the names of the men "lynched at Bernalillo" on Tuesday night. It identified them as Pantaleon Miera of Algodones and Santos Benavides of the north end of Bernalillo, and gave no cause, participants or scene. Dispatches from Albuquerque in February 1881 stated that Miera had been hanged by "vigilantes" or "the vigilants" at Bernalillo for horse stealing. No accusation against Benavides appears in the coverage.

At the end of January 1881, Sheriff Armijo of Bernalillo County arrested several men for the October 1880 murder and robbery of Potter, and their reported confessions named Miera among the killers. A Santa Fe account said that the gang's leader, Marino Leyba, had given Potter's watch to Miera, who pawned it in Albuquerque. No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution for the Bernalillo hanging was found.

Only the Las Vegas Gazette reported the lynching when it happened, and only as a brief local item without comment. Outside New Mexico, Miera's death surfaced as an aside in wire stories about Potter's murder and the jail lynching of three other suspects at Albuquerque. The St. Louis wire carried by the New York Sun and the Portland Daily Press said only that "one of the murderers was hanged a few days ago for horse stealing," and the New-York Tribune's Washington report spoke of an offence "committed since the murder."

The Dallas Daily Herald called Miera "another Mexican" who had shared in the murder and predicted that "if public sentiment goes for anything" his alleged accomplices would follow him. The name was badly garbled in transmission, appearing as "Liena," "Siera," "Liera" and "Pintleton Mira," and none of the later stories mentioned Benavides.

The timing given in later reports varied, from "a few days ago" in the St. Louis wire to "two Weeks Ago" in a Gazette headline and "a few weeks ago" in the Dallas Herald, while the contemporary Gazette item fixed it on Tuesday night, December 28. The River Falls Journal's account placed Miera at Bernalillo "on charge of murder and theft," a garbled clause that differs from the horse-stealing accusation in the other reports.
